records.themeTitle: Creation leaves a task for the human being to complete
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok reads circumcision as evidence that creation intentionally leaves room for human service. Beit Yaakov explains why Abraham waited for a divine command before undertaking that completion.
records.originHebrew: שֶׁהֶרְאָה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ בְּרִיאַת גּוּף הָאָדָם לֹא נִשְׁלַם עֲדַיִן בַּבְּרִיאָה וְצָרִיךְ תִּיקּוּן עַל יְדֵי הָאָדָם.
records.originEnglish: God showed that even the creation of the human body was not yet complete at its creation and required rectification by the human being.
records.targetRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 42:5
records.targetHebrew: וּלְהָבִין הָעִנְיָן: לָמָּה לֹא מָל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ אֶת עַצְמוֹ קוֹדֶם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לוֹ מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, מֵאַחַר שֶׁקִּיֵּים כָּל הַתּוֹרָה כֻּלָּהּ, כִּדְאִיתָא בַּשַּׁ"ס (יוֹמָא כח עַמּוּד ב)ֵ?! אָכֵן הָיָה יָרֵא לְנַפְשׁוֹ לְשַׁנּוֹת אֶבְרֵי הַגּוּף, שֶׁנִּרְאֶה מִזֶּה כְּאוֹמֵר שֶׁיֵּשׁ חִסָּרוֹן בְּשֹׁרֶשׁ הַבְּרִיאָה וּצְרִיכָה תִּיקּוּן, וְהָוֵי כְּאוֹמֵר לָאוּמָּן: "כַּמָּה מְכֹעָר כְּלִי זֶה שֶׁעָשִׂיתָ!" (תַּעֲנִית כ עַמּוּד ב). וַאֲבוֹתֵינוּ הַקְּדוֹשִׁים עָמְדוּ בִּתְמִידוּת נוֹכַח הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ פָּנִים בְּפָנִים; לָכֵן לֹא מָל עַצְמוֹ עַד שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ מַאֲמַר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְפוֹרָשׁ, שֶׁרָמַז לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהִנִּיחַ זֶה הַמָּקוֹם לָאָדָם לְהִתְגַּדֵּר בּוֹ וּלְתַקֵּן אֶת עַצְמוֹ. וְכִדְאִיתָא עַל זֶה בְּתַנְחוּמָא (תַּזְרִיעַ סימן ה): שֶׁמַּעֲשֵׂה בְּנֵי אָדָם נָאִים מִמַּעֲשֵׂה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא; וְהוּא שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּרָא אֶת הָאָדָם שֶׁהָרְשׁוּת נְתוּנָה בְּיָדוֹ וְיָכוֹל לְהִתְפַּשֵּׁט כִּרְצוֹן לִבּוֹ, וְהָאָדָם מִצִּדּוֹ יְצַמְצֵם אֶת עַצְמוֹ, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יוּכַל לְקַבֵּל הַשְׁפָּעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְבוֹרָר, וְהַהוֹלָדָה אֲשֶׁר יוֹלִיד תִּהְיֶה בִּנְיַן עֲדֵי עַד וְיִצְמַח מֵהֶם כְּבוֹד שָׁמַיִם.
records.targetEnglish: To understand the matter: Why did Abraham our father not circumcise himself before God told him to do so, since he fulfilled the entire Torah, as stated in the Talmud? He was afraid to alter the limbs of his body, since this appeared to say that there was a deficiency at the root of creation and that it required correction. It would be like saying to a craftsman, “How ugly is this vessel you made!” Our holy forefathers stood continually before God, face to face. Therefore, he did not circumcise himself until he had an explicit divine command, through which God indicated that He had left this area for a person to exercise his own responsibility and rectify himself. Concerning this, Tanchuma states that human deeds are more beautiful than the deeds of the Holy One, blessed be He. God created the human being with freedom in his hand and the ability to extend himself as his heart desires; the person, for his part, restrains himself. Through this he can receive God’s influence in a clarified form, and the offspring he produces will be an enduring structure from which the glory of Heaven will grow.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov distinguishes a defect imagined by the observer from an unfinished task deliberately entrusted by the Creator. The command reveals that human restraint belongs to the intended completion of creation. This makes Rav Tzadok’s transition from circumcision to weekday spiritual labor more precise: the work fulfills the divine purpose already present in creation.

records.themeTitle: An act of charity can bring the hidden will for good into action
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok finds a surviving good root even in a person whose conduct has deteriorated. An act of tzedakah or kindness can give that hidden root practical expression.
records.originHebrew: אֲפִילּוּ מֵהַיּוֹתֵר גְּרוּעִים בְּתַכְלִית יֵשׁ בָּהֶם אֵיזֶה שׁוֹרֶשׁ טוֹב בְּהֶעְלֵם הַנָּטוּעַ מֵאֲבוֹתָם, בִּהְיוֹתָם זֶרַע אַבְרָהָם יִצְחָק וְיַעֲקֹב, שֶׁיָּצָא לַפּוֹעַל בְּאֵיזֶה מַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁל צְדָקָה אוֹ גְּמִילוּת חֲסָדִים שֶׁעָשָׂה מִיָּמָיו לְנֶפֶשׁ אַחַת מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל,
records.originEnglish: Even among the very worst, there is some good root hidden within them, planted by their forefathers, since they are the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It will emerge in some act of charity or kindness that the person has performed during his life for another Jew.
records.targetHebrew: וּלְדִבְרֵי הַכֹּל הָאוֹמֵר "סֶלַע זוֹ לִצְדָקָה בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁיִּחְיֶה וְכוּ׳" הֲרֵי זֶה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר (פְּסָחִים ח׳ עַמּוּד א׳), אַף דִּלְהַנָּאַת עַצְמוֹ מִתְכַּוֵּן, כָּל דְּדַעְתּוֹ לְמִצְוָה הָוֵי לֵיהּ כַּוָּנָה הַמּוֹעֶלֶת גַּם לְמַאן דְּאָמַר "מִצְוֹת צְרִיכוֹת כַּוָּנָה", וְסַגִּי בְּהָכִי לִהְיוֹת צַדִּיק גָּמוּר. וּפֵרֵשׁ בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה [ד׳ עַמּוּד א׳] דְּהוּא רַק בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, עַיֵּן שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ"י שֶׁלִּבָּם לַשָּׁמַיִם וְכוּ׳; וְהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמַר רַמְבַּ"ם [פֶּרֶק ב׳ מֵהִלְכוֹת גֵּרוּשִׁין] בְּטַעַם "כּוֹפִין עַד שֶׁיֹּאמַר רוֹצֶה אֲנִי", דִּבְמַעֲמַקֵּי לֵב כָּל אֶחָד רוֹצֶה לִשְׁמוֹעַ דִּבְרֵי חֲכָמִים, רַק הַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִסָּה מְעַכֵּב, וּמִשֶּׁהֻכָּה וְתָשַׁשׁ כֹּחַ יִצְרוֹ עַד שֶׁאוֹמֵר בַּפֶּה גַּם כֵּן "רוֹצֶה אֲנִי" — סַגִּי, עַיֵּן שָׁם. וְהָכִי נַמִּי הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא מִצַּד הַיֵּצֶר הַמַּרְגִּילוֹ לְבַקֵּשׁ בְּכָל דָּבָר הֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ, אֲבָל מַעֲמַקֵּי לֵב דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם בִּלְבַד, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב [בְּרָכוֹת י״ז עַמּוּד א׳]: "גָּלוּי וְיָדוּעַ שֶׁרְצוֹנֵנוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹנְךָ וְכוּ׳ וּמִי מְעַכֵּב? שְׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִסָּה", וּכְשֶׁיֵּשׁ מַעֲשֶׂה בְּפֹעַל גַּם כֵּן סַגִּי בְּהָכִי לְהִצְטָרֵף לָרָצוֹן שֶׁבְּמַעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב, וְאֵין מַשְׁגִּיחִין לְמַחֲשֶׁבֶת שְׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִסָּה הַמְעַרְבֶּבֶת.
records.targetEnglish: According to everyone, one who says, “This coin is for charity so that [my son] may live,” and so forth, is fully righteous [in this act], even though he intends his own benefit. As long as he intends a mitzvah, he has an effective intention even according to the view that mitzvot require intention; this suffices for him to be fully righteous [in this act]. Rosh Hashanah explains that this applies specifically to Israel; see Rashi there, who explains that their hearts are directed to Heaven. This follows Rambam’s explanation of “He is compelled until he says, ‘I am willing’”: in the depths of his heart everyone wishes to obey the Sages, but the leaven in the dough obstructs him. Once he has been struck and the force of his inclination weakened until he also says aloud, “I am willing,” that suffices. So too, a Jew’s self-interested intention comes from the inclination that trains him to seek personal benefit in everything. But the depths of Israel’s heart are directed solely to Heaven, as they say: “It is revealed and known that our will is to do Your will. What obstructs us? The leaven in the dough.” When there is also an actual deed, this suffices to join with the will in the depths of the heart; the disturbing thought of the leaven in the dough is disregarded.
records.explanation: Divrei Soferim explains how a concrete charitable act can connect with a deeper intention obscured by mixed motives. This supplies a mechanism for the hidden ancestral root becoming visible in the deed described here. The same paragraph concludes that a person must strive for intention for the sake of Heaven; the recognition of an inner good will strengthens that responsibility.

records.themeTitle: Standing before the King means directing both mind and heart
records.themeSummary: The labor of prayer culminates in awareness of the One before whom a person stands. Rav Tzadok elsewhere describes the inner discipline that makes this awareness possible.
records.originHebrew: וְזֶהוּ הָעֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב, דְּהָעִיקָּר לֵידַע לִפְנֵי מִי הוּא מִתְפַּלֵּל, וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה כְּעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה.
records.originEnglish: This is the service of the heart: its essence is to know before whom one is praying and to be like one standing before the King, as our Sages taught.
records.targetHebrew: עִיקַּר מִלְחֶמֶת הָאָדָם עִם יִצְרוֹ הוּא בַּדִּמְיוֹנוֹת וְהִרְהוּרִים שֶׁבַּלֵּב וָמוֹחַ, וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ בַּתִּיקּוּנִים (סוֹף תִּיקּוּן יג וְרֵישׁ תִּיקּוּן כא): מַאן דְּנָצַח בִּקְרָבָא יְהִיבִין לֵיהּ בְּרַתָּא דְּמַלְכָּא – דָּא צְלוֹתָא. שֶׁהַתְּפִלָּה הוּא הַכָּרַת הַנּוֹכַח וּכְעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּעֵירוּבִין (סד.), וְהַיְינוּ עֲמִידַת הַלֵּב וְהַמּוֹחַ, דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב, וְאִם חַס וְשָׁלוֹם יֶאֱרַע לוֹ אֵיזֶה מַחֲשָׁבָה זָרָה וְהִרְהוּר חִיצוֹנִי, הֲרֵי אֵינוֹ עוֹמֵד בְּאוֹתוֹ רֶגַע לְפָנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ. וְהַמְנַצֵּחַ לְיִצְרוֹ לָצֵאת מִן הַדִּמְיוֹן וּמַחְשֶׁבֶת חוּץ, יְהִיבִין לֵיהּ וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נוֹכַח עֵינָיו בְּעֵת הַתְּפִלָּה; וְזֶהוּ סְמִיכַת גְּאוּלָּה לִתְפִלָּה, דִּגְאֻלַּת מִצְרַיִם הַיְינוּ יְצִיאָה מִדִּמְיוֹן כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
records.targetEnglish: The principal battle of a person against his inclination concerns the imaginings and thoughts in his heart and mind. Concerning this the Tikkunim say: “One who wins the battle is given the King’s daughter”—this is prayer. Prayer is awareness of the One present before him, like standing before the King, as stated in Eruvin. This means the standing of the heart and mind, for God looks into the heart. If, Heaven forbid, an alien thought or an external reflection occurs to him, then at that moment he is not standing before Him. One who conquers his inclination and emerges from imagination and extraneous thought is granted this gift: God is present before his eyes during prayer. This is the joining of redemption to prayer, for redemption from Egypt means emerging from illusion, as explained above.
records.explanation: The parallel gives content to the phrase “service of the heart.” Standing before God requires the attention of mind and heart together; the posture expresses an inward awareness. Rav Tzadok’s connection between redemption and prayer also explains why the work of freeing thought from distraction prepares the encounter described here.

records.themeTitle: The scholar’s Shabbos rest receives the light prepared through effort
records.themeSummary: For the scholar immersed in Torah throughout the week, Rav Tzadok describes a Shabbos ascent to inward reception and closeness to God. His account in Tzidkat HaTzadik locates that ascent within the weekly rhythm of Torah and prayer.
records.originHebrew: כִּי יוּכַל לְהִתְדַּבֵּק אָז בְּאוֹר פְּנֵי מֶלֶךְ חַיִּים מַמָּשׁ,
records.originEnglish: For he can then cleave to the very light of the countenance of the living King.
records.targetHebrew: וּבְכָל יְמֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה הוּא זְמַן הָעֲבוֹדָה בְּעִיּוּן וִיגִיעָה בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה וְעִיּוּן תְּפִלָּה. וּבָא שַׁבָּת בָּא מְנוּחָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּשַׁבָּת (קיט רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב): בְּמָטוּתָא מִינַּיְיכוּ לָא תְּחַלְּלוּנִי; גַּם עַל יְדֵי לִמּוּד תּוֹרָה בִּיגִיעָה נִקְרָא חִלּוּל, כִּי אָז הוּא מְנוּחָה וּמֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא, שֶׁנֶּהֱנִין מִזִּיו מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּעַצְמוֹ מַשְׁפִּיעַ לָהֶם. בַּלַּיְלָה הוּא חֲקַל תַּפּוּחִין – פֵּירוּשׁ הַחֵשֶׁק שֶׁהוּא מִדַּת נוּקְבָא כַּנּוֹדָע; וּבַיּוֹם עַתִּיקָא קַדִּישָׁא הוּא מִדַּת אַיִן, פֵּירוּשׁ הֶעְדֵּר הַחֵשֶׁק, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר בְּשַׁלַּח (נב עַמּוּד ב) עַל "מַה תִּצְעַק אֵלָי" – בְּעַתִּיקָא תַּלְיָא, שֶׁהוּא הַשְׁפָּעָה בְּשׁוֹרֶשׁ נֶפֶשׁ הָאָדָם שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מֵהַשָּׂגוֹת הַמּוּרְגָּשׁוֹת בְּחָכְמָה שֶׁבַּמּוֹחַ וְחֵשֶׁק שֶׁבַּלֵּב.
records.targetEnglish: During all the weekdays it is the time for work, through examination and exertion in words of Torah and the contemplation of prayer. When Shabbos comes, rest comes, as stated in Shabbat: “I ask you, do not desecrate it.” Even Torah study undertaken with exertion is called desecration, for then there is rest and a foretaste of the World to Come: they enjoy the radiance that God Himself bestows upon them. At night it is the field of apples—meaning desire, the feminine attribute, as is known. By day it is Atika Kadisha, the attribute of ayin, meaning the absence of desire, as the Zohar on Beshalach explains concerning “Why do you cry out to Me?”—the matter depends upon Atika. This is an influence upon the root of the human soul, above the apprehensions experienced as wisdom in the mind and desire in the heart.
records.explanation: The source explains the change from the weekday’s striving to the reception of divine radiance. Its contrast between felt desire and the soul’s deeper root clarifies why the present paragraph describes an inward revelation that cannot fully be expressed aloud. Kedushas Shabbos explicitly addresses the scholar whose weekday thoughts are immersed in Torah and affirms Torah study for the wider public; the passage should be read within those stated conditions.

records.themeTitle: Receiving the gift includes recognizing the source of one’s recognition
records.themeSummary: Shabbos is already sanctified by God, while a person’s preparation determines how its holiness is received. Beit Yaakov adds that the awareness through which one receives the gift is itself granted by God.
records.originHebrew: מִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין הָאָדָם מַשִּׂיג קְדֻשָּׁתוֹ אֶלָּא כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּא כְּלִי מוּכָן לְקַבֵּל.
records.originEnglish: Nevertheless, a person apprehends its holiness only to the extent that he is a vessel prepared to receive.
records.targetHebrew: וְזֶה דְּאִיתָא בַּשַּׁ״ס (שַׁבָּת י עַמּוּד ב): מַתָּנָה טוֹבָה יֵשׁ לִי בְּבֵית גְּנָזַי וְשַׁבָּת שְׁמָהּ, לֵךְ וְהוֹדִיעָם; וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל יֵדְעוּ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְקַדְּשָׁם, כִּדְכְתִיב (שְׁמוֹת לא, יג): "לָדַעַת כִּי אֲנִי ה' מְקַדִּשְׁכֶם"; וּמִזֶּה סִימָן שֶׁשַּׁבָּת הִיא טוֹבָה הַרְבֵּה וּגְדוֹלָה, וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁאָמַר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ "לֵךְ וְהוֹדִיעָם", כִּי עִיקָּר הוּא הַהַכָּרָה; וּכְשֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל רוֹצִים לִטְעוֹם מִקְּדֻשַּׁת שַׁבָּת מוּכְרָחִים לִיתֵּן גַּם הַהַכָּרָה שֶׁלָּהֶם לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְזֶה נִקְרָא "אַיִן".
records.targetEnglish: This is what is stated in the Talmud: “I have a good gift in My treasury, and Shabbos is its name; go and inform them.” This means that Israel should know that God sanctifies them, as it says: “To know that I am the Lord who sanctifies you.” This indicates that Shabbos is an exceedingly great good. God’s saying, “Go and inform them,” means that the essential matter is recognition. When Israel wishes to taste the holiness of Shabbos, they must also surrender their own recognition to God. This is called ayin.
records.explanation: The broader Beit Yaakov passage first requires a person to refine himself as far as his understanding can reach. Its Shabbos teaching then places even that understanding within God’s gift. This illuminates the two sides of Rav Tzadok’s account: preparation is required, while the sanctity received and the capacity to recognize its source remain divine gifts.

records.themeTitle: The first flash calls for an immediate response and lasting work
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok describes the first awakening from above as a flash that soon disappears. Its purpose is to move the person toward making the holiness enduring within him.
records.originHebrew: וְהוּא כְּמַרְאֵה הַבָּזָק שֶׁהָאוֹר מֵאִיר כְּרֶגַע וּמִיָּד נֶעְלָם, וְהוּא רַק לְעוֹרֵר הָאָדָם עַל יְדֵי אוֹתוֹ אוֹר מוּעָט כְּמוֹ רֶגַע שֶׁיָּשִׂים אֶל לִבּוֹ לִרְאוֹת שֶׁיִּהְיֶה זֶה כֵּן אֶצְלוֹ בִּקְבִיעוּת.
records.originEnglish: It is like the appearance of lightning: the light shines for a moment and immediately vanishes. It serves to awaken the person through that brief light to consider how this can become established within him permanently.
records.targetHebrew: רֵאשִׁית כְּנִיסַת הָאָדָם לַעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת בְּחִפָּזוֹן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בְּפֶסַח מִצְרַיִם שֶׁהָיָה נֶאֱכָל בְּחִפָּזוֹן, וְלֹא פֶּסַח דּוֹרוֹת. מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהַהַתְחָלָה לְנַתֵּק עַצְמוֹ מִכָּל תַּאֲווֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא מְקֻשָּׁר בָּהֶם, צָרִיךְ לִשְׁמֹר הָרֶגַע שֶׁמִּתְעוֹרֵר בּוֹ רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם, וְלַחְפּוֹז עַל אוֹתוֹ רֶגַע לְמַהֵר לָצֵאת מֵהֶם, אוּלַי יוּכַל. וְאַחַר כָּךְ שׁוּב יֵלֵךְ בִּמְתִינוּת וּלְאַט, כְּדִין פֶּסַח דּוֹרוֹת.
records.targetEnglish: A person’s first entry into the service of God must be in haste, as we find that the Passover offering in Egypt was eaten in haste, whereas the Passover of later generations was not. At the beginning, to detach himself from all the desires of this world to which he is bound, he must preserve the moment in which a desire for God awakens within him and hasten to seize that moment, to hurry out of them if he can. Afterward, he should again proceed with deliberation and slowly, in accordance with the law of the Passover of later generations.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik describes the human response to the fleeting awakening discussed here. The opening moment is guarded through prompt action; the subsequent development proceeds patiently. These are successive stages in making the initial light a lasting acquisition.

records.themeTitle: Shabbos preserves completed service and opens the next stage
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok presents each Shabbos as both the completion of the preceding week and the beginning of the next. Sod Yesharim explains this double role through the changing watches in the Temple.
records.originHebrew: וְכָל שַׁבָּת כֵּן הוּא: אַחֲרוֹן לְשֶׁלְּפָנָיו וְרִאשׁוֹן לְשֶׁלְּאַחֲרָיו,
records.originEnglish: Every Shabbos has this character: it is last in relation to what precedes it and first in relation to what follows it.
records.targetRef: Sod Yesharim, The Night of Shabbat Chol HaMoed Pesach 8:1
records.targetHebrew: וכן בכל שבת קובע השי"ת העבודה של השבוע העבר ומתחיל התחדשות העבודה ולכן תיקנו התחלפות משמורות לכל שבת ולזה נמי הוסיפו ברכה אחת למשמר היונא וכמבואר בגמ' (ברכות י"ב.) מאי ברכה אחת א"ר חלבו משמר היוצא אומר למשמר הנכנס מי ששיכן שמו בבית הזה הוא ישכון ביניכם אהבה ואחוה ושלום וריעית היינו כי משמר היוצא הוא נגד הקדושה שקובע השי"ת בלב האדם מהעבודה שהי' גבי האדם מלפנים קודם השבת לבל יפסיד אותה ח"ו אכן יען שעיקר הנייחה של אדם הוא רק מחדשות נגד זה יש משמר הנכנס להורות שנותן נמי השי"ת חדשות להאדם
records.targetEnglish: Similarly, on every Shabbos God establishes the service of the preceding week and begins the renewal of service. Therefore, they instituted the changing of the watches on every Shabbos. For this reason, they also added one blessing for the departing watch, as explained in Berakhot: What was the additional blessing? Rabbi Chelbo said: The departing watch says to the incoming watch, “May He who caused His name to dwell in this House cause love, brotherhood, peace, and friendship to dwell among you.” The departing watch corresponds to the holiness that God establishes in the heart from the service the person performed before Shabbos, so that he will not lose it, Heaven forbid. Yet because a person’s principal repose comes through newness, corresponding to this is the incoming watch, indicating that God also grants the person something new.
records.explanation: The departing watch gives an image for service that has been secured and preserved; the incoming watch gives an image for new spiritual work. This develops the present phrase “last” and “first” into two distinct gifts of Shabbos. In its original setting the passage also discusses the meeting of Shabbos and festival holiness; the quoted section expressly applies the pattern to every Shabbos.

records.themeTitle: A divine gift can become the recipient’s own Torah
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok invokes Moses’ generosity with Torah to explain how a spiritual gift can be passed to others as their own possession. Divrei Soferim explains what it means for received Torah to become “his Torah.”
records.originHebrew: הַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה שֶׁלָּהֶם בְּמַתָּנָה, שֶׁמַּה שֶּׁיְּחַדְּשׁוּ הֵם בְּפִלְפּוּלָם יִהְיֶה תּוֹרָה שְׁלֵימָה;
records.originEnglish: This means that it would be theirs as a gift, so that what they would innovate through their reasoning would be complete Torah.
records.targetHebrew: וְנִקְרֵאת עַל שְׁמוֹ "תּוֹרַת מֹשֶׁה", כְּאִלּוּ הוּא הַמְחַדְּשָׁהּ מִלִּבּוֹ, כְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁנַּעֲשׂוּ שְׁתֵּי כִלְיוֹתָיו מַעְיָנוֹת נוֹבְעוֹת תּוֹרָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ס״א, שׁוֹחֵר טוֹב א׳), שֶׁעַל יְדֵי יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם כָּל הַתּוֹרָה וְהַחָכְמָה נָתוּן בְּלִבּוֹ וְנוֹבֵעַ מִלִּבּוֹ, כִּי מְכֻוָּן כָּל הַתּוֹרָה לְהַגִּיעַ לְהַשָּׂגַת "אָנֹכִי ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ", וְאָז הַתּוֹרָה וְהַיִּרְאָה בְּקִנְיָן בְּלִבּוֹ תַּרְעָא וְדָרְתָא, וּבִתְחִלַּת הַכְּנִיסָה הוּא לְהֵיפֶךְ.
records.targetEnglish: It is called by his name, “the Torah of Moses,” as though he were bringing it forth anew from his own heart. So too, Abraham our father’s two kidneys became wellsprings flowing with Torah. Through fear of Heaven, all Torah and wisdom are placed in his heart and flow from his heart, for the purpose of the entire Torah is to reach the apprehension of “I am the Lord your God.” Then Torah and fear of Heaven are acquired in his heart, gateway and dwelling; at the beginning of entry, their order is reversed.
records.explanation: The gift brings Torah into an enduring inward possession from which genuine understanding can emerge. This explains the force of “theirs as a gift” in the present argument. Divrei Soferim discusses the gift of Torah; Rav Tzadok’s application of that model to Moses’ gift of Shabbos is made in Kedushas Shabbos itself.

records.themeTitle: Human work prepares the place where blessing takes effect
records.themeSummary: The blessing itself comes from God, yet Rav Tzadok requires a concrete human act upon which it can rest. Beit Yaakov’s image of sowing distinguishes the divine growth from the human preparation that gives it a place.
records.originHebrew: אֶלָּא שֶׁלְּעִנְיַן חָלוּת וְהַשְׁרָאַת הַבְּרָכָה אִי אֶפְשָׁר בְּרֵיקַנְיָא, רַק צָרִיךְ אֵיזֶה דָּבָר בַּפּוֹעַל וּפְעֻלָּה כָּל שֶׁהוּא דְּאָדָם שֶׁעַל זֶה תָּחוּל הַבְּרָכָה, שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רוֹצֶה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הַכֹּל עַל יְדֵי הָאָדָם הֶעָשׂוּי בַּדּוּגְמָא הָעֶלְיוֹנָה.
records.originEnglish: For the blessing to take effect and rest, it cannot do so in emptiness. There must be something actual and some human action upon which the blessing can rest, for God wishes everything to come through the human being made in the supernal likeness.
records.targetHebrew: וּבֶאֱמֶת רוֹאֶה הָאָדָם שֶׁהַגַּרְעִין שֶׁזּוֹרֵעַ בָּאָרֶץ נִפְסָד וְנִרְקָב, כִּי פְּעֻלּוֹת אָדָם הֵם נִפְסָדִים לְגַמְרֵי; אַךְ מִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ הָאָדָם לִזְרוֹעַ. הַאָמְנָם שֶׁפְּעֻלָּתוֹ נִפְסֶדֶת, אָכֵן מוֹעֶלֶת פְּעֻלָּתוֹ לָזֶה: שֶׁכַּאֲשֶׁר יַגִּיעַ הַזְּמַן שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ "מַצְמִיחַ חָצִיר לַבְּהֵמָה וְעֵשֶׂב לַעֲבֹדַת הָאָדָם", מַצְמִיחַ בַּמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה שֶׁהָאָדָם זוֹרֵעַ וְלֹא בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם נִשְׁאַר רֹשֶׁם מֵעֲבוֹדָתוֹ. וְזֶהוּ "זִרְעוּ לָכֶם לִצְדָקָה", כִּי בְּעֵת הַזְּרִיעָה הָאָדָם מוֹסֵר עַצְמוֹ לְגַמְרֵי לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, הַיְינוּ שֶׁיַּפְסִיד כָּל הַזֶּרַע שֶׁזָּרַע; וְעַל כָּל זֶה "קִצְרוּ לְפִי חֶסֶד" – הַיְינוּ שֶׁנּוֹתֵן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יְשׁוּעָה לְהָאָדָם וּמַרְאֶה לוֹ שֶׁהַצְּמִיחָה הִיא בְּאוֹתוֹ מָקוֹם שֶׁזָּרַע וּמֵאוֹתוֹ הַמִּין שֶׁזָּרַע, הַיְינוּ אִם זָרַע חִטִּים יִצְמַח חִטִּים, אִם כֵּן רוֹאֶה שֶׁעַל יְדֵי פְּעֻלָּתוֹ בָּאָה לוֹ הַצְּמִיחָה. וְזֶהוּ "לְפִי חֶסֶד" – שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עוֹשֶׂה חֶסֶד חִנָּם עִם הָאָדָם שֶׁנּוֹתֵן לוֹ בְּמַתָּנָה שֶׁיִּקָּרֵא "יְגִיעַ כַּפַּיִם", וְהוּא בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁהָאָדָם מוֹסֵר עַצְמוֹ לְגַמְרֵי בְּעֵת הַזְּרִיעָה וּמְבַטֵּל פְּעֻלּוֹתָיו לְגַמְרֵי.
records.targetEnglish: A person actually sees that the seed he sows in the earth perishes and decays, for human actions perish completely; nevertheless, he must sow. Although his action perishes, it accomplishes this: when the time arrives for God to “cause grass to grow for the animal and vegetation for the service of man,” He causes it to grow in the place where the person sowed, rather than elsewhere, because a trace of his work nevertheless remains. This is “Sow for yourselves for righteousness”: when sowing, a person entrusts himself entirely to God, accepting that all the seed he has sown will be lost. Despite this, “reap according to kindness”: God sends the person deliverance and shows him that growth comes in the very place he sowed and from the same kind he sowed. If he sowed wheat, wheat grows; thus he sees that the growth came through his action. This is “according to kindness”: God acts with freely given kindness toward the person, granting him the gift that it should be called “the labor of your hands.” This comes because the person entrusted himself entirely to God when sowing and relinquished his claim to his own actions entirely.
records.explanation: The seed does not independently produce the gift of life, yet the place and kind of the eventual growth retain the imprint of the sower’s act. This helps explain Rav Tzadok’s distinction between the blessing’s divine source and the human vessel on which it rests. Beit Yaakov uses the same image to explain prayer offered without treating the requested outcome as a payment owed to the worshipper.

records.themeTitle: Refining desire opens the heart to Torah
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok explains that eating in holiness prepares the heart to receive wisdom. Et HaOchel describes the reciprocal connection between governing desire and filling the heart with Torah.
records.originHebrew: וַ"ה' יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב", שֶׁהָעִיקָּר הוּא זִכּוּךְ הַלֵּב לְקַבֵּל חָכְמָה. וְדָבָר זֶה הוּא עַל יְדֵי אֲכִילָה בִּקְדוּשָּׁה,
records.originEnglish: “The Lord looks into the heart”: the essential matter is the purification of the heart to receive wisdom. This comes through eating in holiness.
records.targetHebrew: וְתַקָּנָה כְּלָלִית לַתַּאֲווֹת הוּא עֵסֶק הַתּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר עַל פָּסוּק "וְעֵץ חַיִּים תַּאֲוָה בָאָה" [מִשְׁלֵי י״ג:י״ב]; וּלְשׁוֹן הָרַמְבַּ״ם בְּהִלְכוֹת אִסּוּרֵי בִּיאָה [פֶּרֶק כ״ב הֲלָכָה כ״א], שֶׁאֵין הַתַּאֲווֹת מְצוּיוֹת אֶלָּא בְּלֵב פָּנוּי מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה; וְזֶהוּ הָרֶמֶז בִּנְטִילַת יָדַיִם קֹדֶם אֲכִילָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר לְעֵיל אוֹת א׳. אָמְנָם הָא בְּהָא תַּלְיָא, וּבְלֵב מָלֵא תַּאֲווֹת וַחֲמוּדוֹת הָעוֹלָם אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה לִכָּנֵס, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמ״ח דְּבָרִים שֶׁהַתּוֹרָה נִקְנֵית, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּעֵירוּבִין [נ״ה עַמּוּד א׳]: אִם מֵשִׂים עַצְמוֹ תַּלְמִיד חָכָם וְכוּלֵי וְאִם לָאו וְכוּלֵי. מִכָּל מָקוֹם דָּבָר זֶה הוּא הָעֵצָה הָרִאשׁוֹנָה לְתַקֵּן עַצְמוֹ בְּתַאֲוֹת לִבּוֹ, וְהוּא הָעִקָּר שֶׁהַכֹּל תָּלוּי בּוֹ;
records.targetEnglish: A general remedy for desires is engagement in Torah, as I have written elsewhere concerning “A desire fulfilled is a tree of life.” Rambam’s wording in the Laws of Forbidden Relations is that desires are found only in a heart empty of words of Torah. This is the allusion of washing the hands before eating, as explained above in section one. Yet the two depend upon one another: words of Torah cannot enter a heart filled with the desires and attractions of this world, as expressed in the forty-eight ways through which Torah is acquired, and as stated in Eruvin: “If he makes himself a Torah scholar,” and so forth, “and if not,” and so forth. Nevertheless, this is the first counsel for rectifying oneself in the desires of the heart, and it is the essential matter upon which everything depends.
records.explanation: The passage makes the preparation described here a relationship working in both directions. Torah helps govern desire, while governing desire makes the heart receptive to Torah. This explains why Rav Tzadok connects the manna and holy eating to the condition of the heart before the giving of the Torah.

records.themeTitle: Recognizing a deficiency creates the vessel for Torah
records.themeSummary: The struggle with good and evil gives human beings a distinctive task in uncovering Torah. Machshavot Charutz explains how awareness of a deficiency can itself prepare a person to receive wisdom.
records.originHebrew: וְדָבָר זֶה בָּא וְנִתְחַדֵּשׁ רַק עַל יְדֵי הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע שֶׁיֵּשׁ הִתְלַבְּשׁוּת דְּטוֹב וָרָע, וּצְרִיכִים הַמַּיְמִינִים לִבְרוֹר דֶּרֶךְ צַדִּיקִים וְדֶרֶךְ רְשָׁעִים שֶׁלֹּא יִכָּשְׁלוּ בָּם. וְעַל כֵּן אֵין לָזֶה שַׁיָּיכוּת לַמַּלְאָכִים שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם יֵצֶר הָרָע.
records.originEnglish: This came into being only through the evil inclination, because there is an embodiment of good and evil, and those who take the right course must distinguish the way of the righteous from the way of the wicked so that they do not stumble. Therefore, this has no application to angels, who have no evil inclination.
records.targetHebrew: כִּי כָּל הַשָּׂגַת אָדָם אֵין בּוֹ שְׁלֵימוּת, דְּכוּלּוֹ מָלֵא חֶסְרוֹנוֹת וְכָל הַשָּׂגָתוֹ הוּא רַק מִצַּד זֶה שֶׁתְּשׁוּקָתוֹ לְמִילּוּי חֶסְרוֹנוֹתָיו, דְּבַעַל חִסָּרוֹן מִשְׁתּוֹקֵק לְהַשְׁלָמָה וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ קַמָּאֵי בְּטַעַם מִדּוֹת הָאָרוֹן הַכֹּל חֲצָאִים שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַכְּלִי קִיבּוּל לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה א:ב) דְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה מַנִּיחִים מָקוֹם גָּבוֹהַּ וְהוֹלְכִים לְמָקוֹם נָמוּךְ וּבְתַעֲנִית (ז׳ רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳): ״דְּאִי הָווּ סָנוּ הָווּ גְּמִירֵי טְפֵי״ וְהַכַּוָּונָה עַל כֵּיעוּר נַפְשׁוֹ מִצַּד הַחֶסְרוֹנוֹת שֶׁבְּשָׁרְשׁוֹ דְּעַל כֵּן נִיתְּנָה תּוֹרָה לִבְנֵי אָדָם וְלֹא לְמַלְאָכִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּפֶרֶק רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא (שַׁבָּת פ״ט עַמּוּד א׳) דְּאָמַר לָהֶם: ״כְּלוּם יֵצֶר רָע יֵשׁ בֵּינֵיכֶם״ וְעַל כֵּן ״לֹא בַשָּׁמַיִם הִוא״ (דְּבָרִים ל:יב) דְּעִיקַּר הַשָּׂגַת דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה הוּא רַק מִצַּד מַה שֶּׁמַּכִּיר חֶסְרוֹנוֹ וְשֶׁצָּרִיךְ הַשְׁלָמָה עַל יְדֵי הַדְּבֵיקוּת בְּקוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהוּא הַמַּשְׁלִימוֹ וּ״כְשֶׁאֲנִי לְעַצְמִי — מָה אֲנִי״ (אָבוֹת א:יד), וְהוּא כְּמוֹ פְּלַג גּוּף
records.targetEnglish: No human apprehension possesses completeness, for a person is full of deficiencies, and all his apprehension comes through his longing to fill those deficiencies: someone who lacks something longs for completion. As earlier authorities explain concerning the Ark’s dimensions, which are all halves, this is the vessel for receiving words of Torah. It follows the teaching that words of Torah leave a high place and go to a low place, and the statement in Taanit, “Had they been unattractive, they would have learned more.” The meaning concerns the soul’s unattractiveness through the deficiencies at its root. Therefore, the Torah was given to human beings and not to angels, as Moses said to them: “Is there an evil inclination among you?” Therefore, “It is not in heaven”: the essential apprehension of words of Torah comes precisely from a person’s recognizing his deficiency and his need for completion through cleaving to his Creator, who completes him. “When I am for myself, what am I?” He is like half a body.
records.explanation: The parallel explains why human limitation can prepare a person for the Torah’s work of clarification. Awareness of what needs repair creates longing and humility, represented by the Ark’s fractional dimensions. Rav Tzadok is describing the spiritual use of an existing deficiency; the passage’s continuation also requires each person to seek understanding appropriate to his capacity.

records.themeTitle: The labor of Oral Torah identifies desires that obscure God’s will
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok compares the labor of Oral Torah to the weekdays sustained by Shabbos. Ohr Zarua LaTzadik identifies a central content of that labor: discerning how competing desires enter human conduct.
records.originHebrew: וְהַיְינוּ לְאַשְׁמְעִינַן דְּאֶצְלֵנוּ קַבָּלַת הַתּוֹרָה לַעֲמַל פֶּה בִּיגִיעַת לֵב וּבָשָׂר בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, לְהָבִין וּלְהַשְׂכִּיל וְלַעֲמוֹד עַל הַמִּסְטוֹרִין וּמַעֲמַקִּים שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה.
records.originEnglish: This teaches that our reception of Torah is for the labor of the mouth, through the exertion of heart and body in the Oral Torah, to understand, gain insight, and reach the secrets and depths of the Torah.
records.targetRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 6:9
records.targetHebrew: וּלְכָךְ תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב הִיא מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁהוּא מְסֻלָּק מִכָּל רָע, רַק מֵאִיר אֵיךְ לְהֵיטִיב. וְתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה — מִלִּבּוֹת בְּנֵי אָדָם, שֶׁהֵם בַּעֲלֵי יֵצֶר לֵב רָע וְיוֹדְעִים בְּטוֹב וָרָע [וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא (שַׁבָּת פ״ט עַמּוּד א׳): קִנְאָה יֵשׁ בֵּינֵיכֶם וְכוּלֵי], הֵם יוֹדְעִים לְצַחְצֵחַ עִנְיַן "לֹא יִהְיֶה", וּלְבָרֵר אֵיזֶה דָבָר הוּא הִשְׁתַּעְבְּדוּת לִתְשׁוּקָה וְרָצוֹן זוּלַת רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
records.targetEnglish: Therefore, the Written Torah is from Heaven, from God, who is removed from all evil; it illuminates how to do good. The Oral Torah comes from human hearts, which possess an inclination toward evil and know good and evil, as the Sages say: “Is there jealousy among you?” They know how to clarify the matter of “You shall have no other gods,” and to determine what constitutes enslavement to a desire and will other than the will of God.
records.explanation: This gives a specific task to the “labor of heart and body” described here: exposing the ways in which a person’s desires can take the place of God’s will. The surrounding passage associates the received beginning with “I am the Lord your God” and human clarification with “You shall have no other gods.” It also expressly recognizes that Written Torah contains both positive and negative commandments; the contrast describes the distinctive work of reception and interpretation.

records.themeTitle: Receiving a given holiness still requires a prepared heart
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok distinguishes the holiness already present in Shabbat from its entry into a person’s heart. Sod Yesharim explains what human preparation contributes when the light itself comes from God.
records.originHebrew: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁקְּדֻשַּׁת הַשַּׁבָּת קְבִיעָא מֵעַצְמָהּ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם שֶׁתִּכָּנֵס בְּלֵב אָדָם צָרִיךְ לִפְעֻלַּת אָדָם וְאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּילֵיהּ: וּבַיּוֹם עַל יְדֵי הַשְּׁבִיתָה שֶׁשּׁוֹבֵת וְאֵין עוֹשֶׂה מַעֲשָׂיו כִּבְחוֹל נַעֲשֶׂה כְּלִי קִבּוּל לְהַקְּדוּשָּׁה; וּבַלַּיְלָה צָרִיךְ לְקַדְּשׁוֹ בַּפֶּה, לִהְיוֹת הוּא הַמְּעוֹרֵר וּמַכְנִיס הַקְּדוּשָּׁה בַּלֵּב.
records.originEnglish: Although the holiness of Shabbat is established of itself, its entry into a person’s heart nevertheless requires human action and that person’s awakening. By day, through resting and refraining from the work he performs on a weekday, he becomes a vessel to receive the holiness; at night, he must sanctify it verbally, himself awakening and bringing the holiness into his heart.
records.targetRef: Sod Yesharim, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot 6:2
records.targetHebrew: שבת עלאה רומז על האור שהוא מצד השי"ת, ושבת תתאה רומז על הכנת האדם שמכין עצמו להכיר בתפיסת דעתו את האור של שבת עלאה כי ע"י ששובת האדם בשבת תתאה יהיה מנחיל לו השי"ת שבת עלאה. אכן במה נחשב כל הכנת אדם נגד זה האור הנעלה משבת עלאה שהוא מצד השי"ת. אמנם עיקר המכוון מאותה הכנה הנקרא שבת תתאה הוא רק כדי שיהיה אצל האדם לדעת כי אני ה' מקדשכם וכפי ההכנה שמכין אדם א"ע שיהיה בו לדעת כי אני ה' מקדשכם כך ינחיל לו השי"ת חלק וקנין בשבת עלאה
records.targetEnglish: “The higher Shabbat” alludes to the light that comes from God; “the lower Shabbat” alludes to the preparation a person makes to recognize, within the grasp of his own understanding, the light of the higher Shabbat. Through a person’s resting in the lower Shabbat, God will grant him the higher Shabbat as an inheritance. Yet what can all human preparation amount to beside this exalted light of the higher Shabbat, which comes from God? The principal purpose of that preparation, called the lower Shabbat, is that the person should attain “to know that I am the Lord who sanctifies you.” According to the preparation a person makes so that this knowing—“that I am the Lord who sanctifies you”—should be present in him, God grants him a share and an acquired possession in the higher Shabbat.
records.explanation: The comparison identifies receptivity as a form of knowledge: through observance, the person comes to recognize the One who sanctifies him and receives the gift as his own. This explains why Rav Tzadok can affirm both that Shabbat’s holiness is already fixed and that an awakening from the person is necessary. Sod Yesharim supplies this general account of preparation and reception; Rav Tzadok’s particular distinction between daytime cessation and nighttime Kiddush remains the argument of the present passage.

records.themeTitle: Repentance revisits the past without canceling present responsibility
records.themeSummary: The Minchah discussion locates choice before an act and the repairing disclosure of divine knowledge after it. Tzidkat HaTzadik states explicitly why these two perspectives must each retain its own place.
records.originHebrew: וְהַיְינוּ כַּיָּדוּעַ בְּסוֹד הַיְדִיעָה וְהַבְּחִירָה דִּשְׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת: וּבָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה מְשַׁמֶּשֶׁת הַבְּחִירָה, וְזֶהוּ קוֹדֶם הַמַּעֲשֶׂה; אֲבָל אַחַר כָּךְ, דְּמַה שֶּׁעָבַר כְּבָר אֵינֶנּוּ וְאֵינוֹ עוֹד בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, יוּכַל לְתַקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם עַל יְדֵי הִתְגַּלּוּת אוֹר הַיְדִיעָה שֶׁהוּא לְמַעְלָה מֵעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, שֶׁשָּׁם אֵין מָקוֹם לַבְּחִירָה, וְיִתְגַּלֶּה דְּהַכֹּל מֵה'.
records.originEnglish: This is as is known concerning the mystery of divine knowledge and human choice: both are true. In this world, choice operates, and this is before the act. Afterward, however, what has passed is already gone and is no longer in this world; one can repair what came before through the revelation of the light of divine knowledge, which is above this world, where there is no place for choice, and it will be revealed that everything is from the Lord.
records.targetHebrew: עִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא עַד שֶׁיָּאִיר ה' עֵינָיו שֶׁיִּהְיוּ זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁיַּכִּיר וְיָבִין שֶׁכָּל מַה שֶּׁחָטָא הָיָה גַּם כֵּן בִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת לא סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): ג' פְּסוּקִים וְכוּלֵי, "וְאַתָּה הֲסִבֹּתָ אֶת לִבָּם אֲחֹרַנִּית", "וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי" וְכוּלֵי. וּכְטַעַם יְדִיעָה וּבְחִירָה שֶׁבֵּיאַר הָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל בְּסוֹף סֵפֶר אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שֶׁקֶל כֶּסֶף, שֶׁשְּׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת, כָּל אֶחָד בְּמָקוֹם בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ: בִּמְקוֹם הַבְּחִירָה שָׁם אֵין מָקוֹם לִידִיעָה, וּבִמְקוֹם הַיְדִיעָה שָׁם בֶּאֱמֶת אֵין מָקוֹם לַבְּחִירָה. וּכְשֶׁמַּשִּׂיג לְאוֹר זֶה הָעָצוּם, אָז שָׁבוּ כָּל זְדוֹנוֹתָיו בִּלְתִּי יוֹצְאִים מֵעוֹמֶק יְדִיעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְהוּא וְדַעְתּוֹ וּרְצוֹנוֹ הַכֹּל אֶחָד.
records.targetEnglish: The essence of repentance is to reach the point at which the Lord illuminates one’s eyes so that deliberate sins become like merits. This means that one recognizes and understands that everything in which one sinned was also within the will of the blessed God, as our Sages said: “Three verses,” and so forth—“You have turned their hearts backward,” “and whom I have afflicted,” and so forth. This accords with divine knowledge and human choice, as the Ari explained at the end of Four Hundred Shekels of Silver: both are true, each in a place of its own. In the place of choice there is no place for divine knowledge, and in the place of divine knowledge there is in truth no place for choice. When a person attains this immense light, all his deliberate sins return to being within the depths of God’s knowledge; and He, His knowledge, and His will are all one.
records.explanation: The source illuminates the precise distinction made here, rather than offering a reason to choose a transgression. It speaks about a repentant person’s recognition of deeds already committed. Rav Tzadok’s present paragraph makes the temporal boundary explicit: before action, the person must choose; afterward, repentance can uncover a relation to God that the sin had concealed. Reading “everything is from God” within that boundary preserves both the possibility of repair and the responsibility that makes repentance necessary.

records.themeTitle: Shabbat sends holiness into the week that follows
records.themeSummary: The remaining impression of Shabbat enables a person to prepare for the next Shabbat at a higher level. Likkutei Maamarim explains the two directions in which Shabbat works upon the surrounding weekdays.
records.originHebrew: וְכֵן הַשַּׁבָּת עִם יְמֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה. וְעַל כֵּן צָרִיךְ לְזָכְרוֹ בְּכָל יוֹם, וּ"מֵחַד בְּשַׁבָּא לְשַׁבְּתָא" (בֵּיצָה טז.), לְהַרְגִּישׁ גַּם בָּהֶם הָרְשִׁימוּ דִּקְדֻשַּׁת שַׁבָּת. דְּעַל יְדֵי הָרְשִׁימוּ הַנִּשְׁאָר בּוֹ מִקְּדֻשַּׁת שַׁבָּת הֶעָבָר, הוּא יָכוֹל לַעֲשׂוֹת הֲכָנָה בְּקִרְבּוֹ לְקַבֵּל קְדֻשַּׁת שַׁבָּת הַבָּאָה בְּיֶתֶר שְׂאֵת;
records.originEnglish: So too with Shabbat and the weekdays. Therefore one must remember it every day, and “from the first day of the week, for Shabbat,” sensing in those days as well the impression of Shabbat’s holiness. Through the impression remaining within him from the holiness of the previous Shabbat, he can prepare himself inwardly to receive the holiness of the coming Shabbat with greater intensity.
records.targetRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:13
records.targetHebrew: כִּי כָל שַׁבָּת נוֹתֵן קְדֻשָּׁה בְּשֵׁשֶׁת יָמִים הֶעָבָר, מִצַּד הֶעָבָר שֶׁכְּבָר נִפְעַל וְאֵינוֹ עוֹד בְּיַד הָאָדָם, לְכָךְ סֵדֶר הַקְּדֻשָּׁה בּוֹ כִּבְרִיָּתוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם: מוֹנֶה שִׁשָּׁה וּמְקַדֵּשׁ שְׁבִיעִי (שַׁבָּת ס״ט עַמּוּד ב׳); וּבַלְּהַבָּא שֶׁהוּא בְּיָדוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם, סֵדֶר הַקְּדֻשָּׁה בּוֹ כְּסִדְרוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן: מְקַדֵּשׁ אֶחָד וּמוֹנֶה שִׁשָּׁה; וּלְכָךְ הַשַּׁבָּת נוֹתֵן קְדֻשָּׁה בַּלְּהַבָּא בְּשֵׁשֶׁת יְמֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה הַבָּאִים. וּקְדֻשַּׁת הַזְּמַנִּים דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל מְקַדְּשֵׁי, הֵם מְקַבְּלִים מִקְּדֻשַּׁת הַשַּׁבָּת דִּקְבוּעָה וְקַיָּימָא.
records.targetEnglish: Every Shabbat imparts holiness to the six days that have passed. Regarding the past, which has already been acted out and is no longer in a person’s hands, its order of holiness follows the order of the world’s creation: one counts six days and sanctifies the seventh. Regarding the future, which is in a person’s hands, its order of holiness follows the order experienced by Adam: one sanctifies one day and then counts six. Thus Shabbat imparts holiness prospectively to the six coming weekdays. The holiness of the appointed times, which Israel sanctifies, is received from the holiness of Shabbat, which is already fixed and enduring.
records.explanation: This gives a reason that remembering Shabbat during the week is more than recalling a finished experience. The coming weekdays receive something from Shabbat and become the arena in which the person acts upon it. The present passage then adds a further step: that received impression becomes preparation for the following Shabbat. Likkutei Maamarim also describes Shabbat’s effect upon the previous week; the emphasis here is its forward movement into weekdays and renewed preparation.

records.themeTitle: Unfelt holiness can still shape a person’s conduct
records.themeSummary: Shabbat can implant holiness even when a person experiences no added feeling of holiness. Beit Yaakov uses the quiet arrival of dew to describe a divine gift whose inward effect is greater than its visible appearance.
records.originHebrew: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין הָאָדָם מַרְגִּישׁ שׁוּם תּוֹסֶפֶת קְדוּשָּׁה בְּעַצְמוֹ וּבְקֶרֶב לִבּוֹ אֲפִילּוּ בְּיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת עַצְמוֹ, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בִּימֵי הַחוֹל שֶׁאַחֲרָיו, הָאֱמֶת כֵּן הוּא מַה שֶּׁהוֹדִיעָנוּ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כִּי הוּא מַכְנִיס קְדוּשָּׁה בְּקִרְבֵּנוּ עַל יְדֵי זֶה, אַף שֶׁאֵינוֹ מוּרְגָּשׁ לָנוּ עַל יְדֵי הָעֲווֹנוֹת הַמַּבְדִּילִים בֵּינֵינוּ לְבֵינוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁהֵם הַמַּאְפִילִים לְאוֹר קְדוּשָּׁה זוֹ שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת לִבּוֹ. אֲבָל אֵינָם פּוֹעֲלִים אֶלָּא הֶעְלֵם, עַל יְדֵי מְחִיצַת הוּצֵי וְחוֹחִים הַסּוֹבְבִים לַהֲדַס וְהַשּׁוֹשַׁנָּה, וְלֹא שֶׁיְּכַבּוּ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם הָאוֹר לְגַמְרֵי.
records.originEnglish: Even though a person feels no additional holiness within himself or in his heart, even on Shabbat itself—and certainly during the weekdays that follow—the truth is as God has informed us: through this He brings holiness into our midst. Although we do not feel it because of the sins that separate us from Him, which darken this light of holiness so that it is not manifest in the heart, they cause only concealment, through the barrier of thorns surrounding the myrtle and the rose; they do not, Heaven forbid, extinguish the light altogether.
records.targetHebrew: וְטַל הוּא שֶׁאֵינוֹ מַרְגִּישׁ הָאָדָם בְּהַשְׁפָּעָתוֹ, לֹא כְּמוֹ גֶּשֶׁם שֶׁמַּרְגִּישׁ הָאָדָם בִּירִידָתוֹ, רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁפִּיעַ בְּצִנְעָה. וּמִצַּד זֶה יֵשׁ לָאָדָם צִמְצוּמִים, כְּמוֹ בְּשַׁבָּת שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נוֹתֵן בּוֹ קְדֻשָּׁה מְאֹד בְּהַצְנֵעַ וְאֵין מַרְגִּישׁ בּוֹ הָאָדָם, וְאָז מִצַּד הָאָדָם צָרִיךְ לְצַמְצֵם עַצְמוֹ בְּכָל לְבוּשִׁים; וְאִם לֹא הָיָה הַקְּדֻשָּׁה שֶׁל שַׁבָּת גְּדוֹלָה כָּל כָּךְ לֹא הָיָה בוֹ כָּל כָּךְ גְּדָרִים, וְרַק לְפִי שֶׁהַלֵּב מַרְגִּישׁ הַפְּנִימִיּוּת שֶׁהוּא מָלֵא טוֹב אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִרְאֶה עַל הַגָּוֶון, לָכֵן יֵשׁ בּוֹ צִמְצוּם. וּכְמוֹ כֵן מִצַּד טַל יֵשׁ לְהָאָדָם צִמְצוּם.
records.targetEnglish: Dew is something whose bestowal a person does not feel, unlike rain, whose descent he feels; rather, God bestows it quietly. From this come restraints for the person, as on Shabbat, when God gives holiness very secretly and the person does not feel it. On the person’s side, he must then restrain himself in all his outward expressions. If Shabbat’s holiness were not so great, it would not have so many boundaries. It is precisely because the heart senses the inwardness, which is full of good although it does not appear on the surface, that there is restraint. In the same way, dew brings a person restraint.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov connects the hidden gift with concrete boundaries of conduct: the absence of an obvious spiritual sensation does not make Shabbat empty. His distinction between the heart’s inward responsiveness and what appears on the surface also helps explain how a person can possess holiness without consciously experiencing its full light. The two passages locate concealment differently. Rav Tzadok here names sins that obscure the light; Beit Yaakov emphasizes the quiet, hidden manner of the gift itself. Their shared point is that outward feeling does not exhaust what Shabbat imparts.

records.themeTitle: Preparation can share a mitzvah’s holiness without sharing every legal power
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok finds genuine mitzvah holiness in devoted preparation, while explicitly preserving the ruling that rejects Rabbi Eliezer’s Shabbat dispensation. Yisrael Kedoshim draws this same distinction between spiritual participation and the power to override a prohibition.
records.originHebrew: וְיֵשׁ כֹּחַ בָּאָדָם לְהַכְנִיס בְּהַהֲכָנָה מִקְּדֻשַּׁת הַמִּצְוָה עַצְמָהּ. וְזֶהוּ טַעַם דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר דְּמַכְשִׁירֵי מִצְוָה דּוֹחֶה שַׁבָּת (שַׁבָּת קל.), שֶׁהוּא הִרְגִּישׁ כְּפִי מַדְרֵגָתוֹ הַגְּדוֹלָה קְדֻשַּׁת הַמִּצְוָה בְּמַכְשִׁירֶיהָ גַּם כֵּן; וְאָמְרוּ (בְּשַׁבָּת קל.): "עִיר שֶׁעָשׂוּ כְּמוֹתָם, מֵתוּ בִּזְמַנָּם וְלֹא הָיָה שְׁמָד דְּמִילָה עֲלֵיהֶם", הֲרֵי שֶׁהִיא מַעֲלָה גְּדוֹלָה. וְעִם כָּל זֶה אֵין הַהֲלָכָה כֵּן, וְהוּא אָסוּר, וְהָעוֹשֶׂה כֵּן מְחַלֵּל שַׁבָּת; דְּהַהִילוּךְ לְהַנְהָגַת עוֹלָם אֵינוֹ כֵן, דְּלֹא כָּל אֶחָד זוֹכֶה לְמַדְרֵגָה זוֹ;
records.originEnglish: A person has the power to bring some of the mitzvah’s own holiness into its preparation. This is the reason for Rabbi Eliezer’s view that preparatory acts for a mitzvah override Shabbat: according to his great spiritual level, he sensed the mitzvah’s holiness in its preparations as well. They said, “In a city that acted according to their view, they died at their appointed time, and no decree against circumcision was imposed upon them”; this is clearly a great distinction. Nevertheless, the halakhah does not follow this view: it is forbidden, and one who does so desecrates Shabbat. The way the world is to be conducted does not follow it, for not everyone attains this level.
records.targetHebrew: וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים לְדִבְרֵי הַכֹּל, גַּם מַכְשִׁירִין גְּמוּרִים אַף שֶׁאֵינָן מִגּוּף הַמִּצְוָה לִדְחוֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה — מִכָּל מָקוֹם שֵׁם מִצְוָה מִיהַת עֲלֵיהֶן כֵּיוָן דְּהֵם הֲכָנָה לַמִּצְוָה; וַהֲרֵי אֲפִילּוּ: ״הַנִּטְפָּל לְעוֹשֵׂי מִצְוָה — כְּעוֹשֵׂי מִצְוָה״, כִּדִתְנַן בְּמַכּוֹת (ה׳ סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳); וְהָכִי נַמֵּי דָּבָר הַנִּטְפָּל לְמַעֲשֵׂה הַמִּצְוָה הוּא כְּמִצְוָה לְהַכְנִיס קְדוּשָׁה בְּלִבּוֹ; שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַקִּבּוּל שָׂכָר דְּ״שְׂכַר מִצְוָה — מִצְוָה״ (אָבוֹת ד:ב); דְּעַל יְדֵי הִתְעוֹרְרוּת הַקְּדוּשָׁה בַּלֵּב מִתְעוֹרֵר לְהוֹסִיף מִצְוֹת.
records.targetEnglish: At any rate, everyone agrees that even acts that are purely preparatory, though they are not part of the mitzvah itself for the purpose of overriding a negative commandment, nevertheless bear the name of mitzvah, since they prepare for a mitzvah. Even “one who attaches himself to those performing a mitzvah is like those performing a mitzvah,” as we learn in Makkot 5b. Similarly, something attached to the act of the mitzvah is like a mitzvah in bringing holiness into the heart. This is the reward meant by “the reward of a mitzvah is a mitzvah” (Avot 4:2): through the awakening of holiness in the heart, a person is stirred to add further mitzvot.
records.explanation: The carefully qualified “at any rate” is central: preparations can have a mitzvah’s name and can awaken holiness even where they lack the legal standing to override a prohibition. This supplies the conceptual basis for sensing Shabbat’s light during Friday’s preparations. It also reinforces the express limit in the present text: Rabbi Eliezer’s spiritual perception does not establish the practical halakhah. The comparison concerns the holiness that preparation brings into the heart; it does not extend a legal dispensation to preparatory acts.

records.themeTitle: Fear tests the direction of even an elevated longing
records.themeSummary: The union of love and fear in Jacob prevents either power from producing a distorted offshoot. Tzidkat HaTzadik explains why even the desire for Torah and knowledge of God requires the restraint of fear.
records.originHebrew: וּשְׁלֵימוּת הָאָדָם הוּא שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כָּלוּל בִּשְׁנֵיהֶם – אַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה. כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיוּ אֲבוֹת הָעוֹלָם אַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק, שֶׁהֵם הַמִּדּוֹת דְּאַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה בְּפֵירוּד, כָּל אֶחָד לְבַדּוֹ – יָצָא עֲדַיִן פְּסֹלֶת. וְאַחַר כָּךְ נוֹלַד יַעֲקֹב, שֶׁהִיא שְׁלֵימוּת צוּרַת אָדָם שֶׁבַּמֶּרְכָּבָה הַכָּלוּל מִשְּׁנֵיהֶם, וְהָיָה מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה, וְהוּא הָיָה הַשְּׁלֵימוּת שֶׁקּוֹדֶם הַחֵטְא.
records.originEnglish: A person’s completeness is to include both qualities—love and fear. With the patriarchs Abraham and Isaac, who embody love and fear separately, each on its own, an impure offshoot still emerged. Afterward Jacob was born, the complete human form in the divine chariot, incorporating both, and his offspring were all whole. He was the completeness that preceded the sin.
records.targetHebrew: רַק שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת בְּחֵשֶׁק הָאָדָם, אֲפִילּוּ לְתוֹרָה וְלִידִיעַת אֱלֹהוּת, מֵאַחַר שֶׁאֵין הַלֵּב נָקִי, הַחֵשֶׁק הַטֶּבַע מִמֶּנּוּ גַּם כֵּן אֵין נָקִי לְגַמְרֵי, וְאֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה תַּאֲוָה כְּכָל הַתַּאֲווֹת וּכְמוֹ שֶׁחוֹשְׁקִין לָדַעַת חָכְמָה וְכַדּוֹמֶה. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל פָּסוּק "לֹא בָרוּחַ ה' וְגוֹמֵר" (מְלָכִים א יט, יא), פֵּירוּשׁ: רָצוֹן וְהִתְלַהֲבוּת בְּאַהֲבָה וְרַעַשׁ בְּיִרְאָה – הַכֹּל עֲדַיִן אֵינוֹ נָקִי וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה מְעוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בּוֹ. וְעַל זֶה הוּא הַיִּרְאָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב שֶׁמַּגְדֶּרֶת הָאַהֲבָה וּמְצַמְצְמַתּוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה רַק מַה שֶּׁהוּא לִכְבוֹד שָׁמַיִם. וְהִתְכַּלְלוּתָם הוּא מִדַּת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הָרוֹמֵז לְשֵׁם הֲוָיָ"ה וְצוּרַת אָדָם שֶׁבַּמֶּרְכָּבָה שֶׁהוּא תַּכְלִית הַשְּׁלֵימוּת.
records.targetEnglish: In truth, however, even a person’s longing for Torah and the knowledge of God is not entirely pure as long as his heart is not pure. His natural longing may be an appetite like other appetites, such as the desire to know a body of wisdom. As I heard concerning the verse, “The Lord was not in the wind,” and so forth: desire and enthusiasm in love, and tumult in fear, are all still not pure, so that they should constitute a dwelling for God. For this there is fear within the heart, which bounds love and restrains it so that it should be only for the honor of Heaven. Their integration is the quality of Jacob our father, peace be upon him, which alludes to the divine name Havayah and the human form in the chariot—the ultimate completeness.
records.explanation: The source makes the need for integration concrete. A powerful desire can take Torah as its object while still carrying the person’s ordinary appetite for possession or achievement. Fear examines and restrains that movement so that love is directed toward Heaven. The quotation also refuses to idealize emotional fear by itself: its tumult can likewise remain unpurified. Jacob’s completeness therefore means that the qualities refine one another; it is not simply a matter of increasing the intensity of either feeling.

records.themeTitle: The use of an appetite’s strength helps disclose whether it was sanctified
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok distinguishes the eventual elevation of bodily appetite from a generation that still requires preparation. In the comparison below, Beit Yaakov has just described eating in holiness and using the strength of that meal for divine service and Torah.
records.originHebrew: וְכַוָּנַת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הָיְתָה בָּזֶה לְהַעֲלוֹת וּלְתַקֵּן גַּם תַּאֲוָה הַגּוּפָנִית, דִּבְשַׁבָּת הַכֹּל נִכְנָס אֶל הַקֹּדֶשׁ, וְכָל יְמוֹת עוֹלָם דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּכָךְ: לְהַעֲלוֹת גַּם דְּבָרִים הַגַּשְׁמִיִּים. אֲבָל בְּדוֹר הַמִּדְבָּר, שֶׁהָיוּ הַתְחָלַת בִּנְיַן הָאוּמָּה הַקְּדוֹשָׁה, רָצָה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לִקְבּוֹעַ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה בְּלִבָּם עַל יְדֵי הַנְהָגָה אַחֶרֶת, וְשֶׁיֹּאכְלוּ רַק לֶחֶם מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם הַמְנוּגָּב מִכָּל תַּאֲוָה גּוּפָנִית;
records.originEnglish: The intention of the children of Israel was to elevate and rectify bodily appetite as well, for on Shabbat everything enters holiness; throughout the ages of this world, God’s will is to elevate material things too. But for the wilderness generation, which was the beginning of the building of the holy nation, God wished to establish words of Torah in their hearts through a different mode of guidance: they were to eat only bread from heaven, entirely free of bodily appetite.
records.targetHebrew: אָז תִּתְבָּרֵר אֲכִילָתוֹ שֶׁהִיא כֻּלּוֹ טוֹב וּלְמִצְוָה מַמָּשׁ תֵּחָשֵׁב. אֲבָל אִם לֹא יַעֲשֶׂה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ, אָז תִּתְבָּרֵר אֲכִילָתוֹ לִהְיוֹת כֻּלּוֹ מֵהַהֵיפֶךְ. וְכֵן בְּכָל דָּבָר שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם יוּכַל לְבָרֵר וּלְהַעֲלוֹת הַכֹּל וּלְקָרֵב כָּל הַדְּבָרִים לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְהַבֵּירוּר הוּא בָּזֶה שֶׁהוּא יַעֲשֶׂה הַטּוֹב אַחַר קַבָּלָתוֹ הַכֹּחַ מִדִּבְרֵי הָרְשׁוּת לְהַעֲלוֹתָם לִקְדוּשָּׁה. וְיַעַן כִּי זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַנְּשָׁמָה הַקְּדוֹשָׁה שֶׁתָּבֹא לָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְבָרֵר אֶת הַקְּלִיפָּה הַזּוֹ וּלְהָאִיר אֶת הַחֹשֶׁךְ שֶׁבָּהּ, לָכֵן הָיָה מֵהַצּוֹרֶךְ לְהַצִּיל אֶת לוֹט, בִּכְדֵי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לְאַבְרָהָם עֵסֶק בַּעֲבוֹדָתוֹ עֲבוֹדַת בּוֹרְאוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ:
records.targetEnglish: Then his eating will be clarified as wholly good and will be considered an actual mitzvah. But if he does not act as we have said, his eating will be clarified as entirely the opposite. So too, in every matter in the world, one can clarify and elevate everything and bring all things near to God. The clarification consists in doing good after receiving strength from matters that are permitted, thereby elevating them to holiness. Since this is the task of the holy soul when it comes into this world—to clarify this kelippah and illuminate its darkness—it was necessary to rescue Lot, so that Abraham would have a sphere of activity in his service of his blessed Creator.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov gives a concrete meaning to elevating the physical: the strength received from permitted food is actually carried into divine service. His preceding paragraph supplies the condition for the quotation’s “then.” This helps the reader understand why the wish to sanctify appetite is not, by itself, its completed sanctification. Rav Tzadok’s additional point is historical and developmental: the wilderness generation first needed the purifying discipline of manna. Beit Yaakov’s account of permitted activity illuminates that goal without removing the preparation Rav Tzadok says was still required.

records.themeTitle: Loving another means experiencing his lack as one’s own
records.themeSummary: Love of God unites a soul with the other souls of Israel, which form one complete organism. Tiferet Yosef shows what this unity means within the concrete practice of prayer.
records.originHebrew: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין מִקְרָא יוֹצֵא מִידֵי פְּשׁוּטוֹ: רֵעֲךָ מַמָּשׁ גַּם כֵּן, וְהַכֹּל אֶחָד; כִּי מִי שֶׁאוֹהֵב הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּכָל לְבָבוֹ וּבְכָל נַפְשׁוֹ וּבְכָל מְאֹדוֹ לְהִתְאַחֵד שׁוֹרֶשׁ נַפְשׁוֹ בִּמְקוֹרָהּ, הִיא מִתְאַחֶדֶת מִמֵּילָא גַּם כֵּן עִם כָּל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהֵם קוֹמָה אַחַת שְׁלֵימָה
records.originEnglish: Nevertheless, Scripture never leaves its plain meaning: it also means your actual fellow, and it is all one. For one who loves God with all his heart, all his soul, and all his might, to unite the root of his soul with its source, thereby unites it also with all the souls of Israel—the root of the congregation of Israel, which is one complete organism.
records.targetHebrew: הנה ענין תפלה הוא אחר שהאדם מכיר את עצמו חסר, ועומד להתפלל לפני השי"ת שישלים את אשר חסר לו. וכן הוא ג"כ ענין של תפלה בצבור, היינו שהמתפלל יכליל בעצמו גם את צרכי חבירו, וירגיש ממילא את חסרונות חבירו ולא יכול להיות מפויס ומרוצה עד שיושלם גם חברו כמותו, ומפני שמרגיש חסרון חבירו אינו מניח לו להיות עומד ומתפלל עד שיכלול גם חבירו בתפלתו, שהשי"ת ישלים גם את חבירו, כי דבר החסר לחבירו חסר גם לו לעצמו. וזה הוא שתיקן האר"י הקדוש ז"ל שקודם התפלה צריך לומר, הריני מקבל על עצמי לקיים מצות עשה של ואהבת לרעך כמוך. וזה הוא מדת האבות, שמכליל בעצמו כל ההסתעפות שנסתעפו מאתו,
records.targetEnglish: Prayer comes after a person recognizes himself as lacking and stands to pray before God that He complete what he lacks. This is also the meaning of communal prayer: the person praying should include his fellow’s needs within himself. He will consequently feel his fellow’s lacks and will be unable to be satisfied or content until his fellow too is made whole like himself. Because he feels his fellow’s lack, it does not allow him to stand and pray without including his fellow in his prayer, asking that God complete his fellow as well; for what his fellow lacks is also lacking to him himself. This is what the holy Ari instituted: before prayer one should say, “I hereby accept upon myself the fulfillment of the positive commandment, ‘You shall love your fellow as yourself.’” This is the quality of the patriarchs: a person includes within himself all the branches that have branched from him.
records.explanation: The language of one organism acquires a practical consequence: another person’s need cannot remain outside my own prayer. This directly supports Rav Tzadok’s insistence that the plain meaning, “your actual fellow,” remains in force even while he explains love through the soul’s divine root. Tiferet Yosef applies the principle to communal prayer and to the patriarchs’ inclusion of their descendants; Rav Tzadok states the more general relation between love of God and love of the souls of Israel.

records.themeTitle: Earthly bread and Oral Torah disclose God through human effort
records.themeSummary: Joshua’s task is to reveal God’s kingship within the land and its desirable material things. Likkutei Maamarim links this transition from manna to earthly bread with the transition from openly given Torah to Torah disclosed through human thought.
records.originHebrew: וּלְתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הָיָה דַּי לָהֶם בְּסֵפֶר יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בְּעֶרְכָּהּ שֶׁל אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁשָּׁם הִתְגַּלּוּת כְּבוֹד מַלְכוּתוֹ שֶׁהוּא מֶלֶךְ הָאָרֶץ וְנִקְרָא "אֱלֹהֵי הָאָרֶץ" (מְלָכִים ב י״ז:כ״ו). וְעַל כֵּן הִתְגַּלּוּת זֶה לֹא הָיָה אֶפְשָׁר עַל יְדֵי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהוּא הָיָה מֶלֶךְ, רַק בְּ"הִתְאַסֵּף רָאשֵׁי עָם יַחַד שִׁבְטֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל" (דְּבָרִים ל״ג:ה׳), בִּהְיוֹתָם בַּמִּדְבָּר בְּקִיבּוּץ אֶחָד בְּלֵב אֶחָד, וְהָיוּ מְנוּגָּבִים שָׁם מִכָּל טוֹבוֹת וְתַאֲווֹת וַחֲמוּדוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה. אֲבָל יְהוֹשֻׁעַ הָיָה מֶלֶךְ הָאָרֶץ, לְהָאִיר לְיִשְׂרָאֵל כִּי "לַה' הָאָרֶץ וּמְלוֹאָהּ", דְּגַם כָּל חֲמוּדוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה יוּכְלוּ לְהַעֲלוֹתָם לִמְקוֹרָם:
records.originEnglish: For the Oral Torah, the book of Joshua, with its account of the Land of Israel, would have sufficed for them. There the glory of His kingship is revealed: He is King of the land and is called “the God of the land.” This revelation could not come through Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, whose kingship existed only “when the heads of the people assembled, the tribes of Israel together,” while they were united in the wilderness with one heart and were entirely removed from the benefits, desires, and delights of this world. Joshua, however, was king of the land: he was to illuminate for Israel that “the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord,” so that all the delights of this world, too, could be elevated to their source.
records.targetRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 11
records.targetHebrew: וְהִיא בְּעִנְיַן חַיּוּת הַנֶּפֶשׁ מַמָּשׁ דֻּגְמַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, שֶׁהִיא חָכְמוֹת שֶׁבְּנֵי אָדָם מוֹלִידִים מֵעַצְמָם מִשִּׂכְלָם, רַק שֶׁיּוֹדְעִים שֶׁהוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְאָז נִקְרָא "תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה"; אֲבָל כְּשֶׁאֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁהוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, אָז נִקְרָא "חָכְמָה חִיצוֹנִית", וְהִיא אֶרֶץ הָעַמִּים. כִּי חַיֵּי הַגּוּף וְחַיֵּי הַנֶּפֶשׁ עִנְיָן אֶחָד, שֶׁהֲרֵי מְלֻבָּשִׁים זֶה בָּזֶה, רַק שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד יֵשׁ לוֹ לְבוּשׁ וְגָוֶן אַחֵר: שֶׁחַיֵּי הַגּוּף הוּא מֵאֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה וְעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ נִבְרָא, וְחַיֵּי הַנֶּפֶשׁ הוּא מֵחָכְמָה וְתוֹרָה שֶׁמִּשָּׁם נִבְרֵאת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר; וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה א׳ [א׳:ב׳]): כָּל אֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה שֶׁבִּמְגִלָּה זוֹ — בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה הַכָּתוּב מְדַבֵּר, שֶׁהִיא מַאֲכַל הַנֶּפֶשׁ. וְכָךְ הָיוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּמִּדְבָּר: מַאֲכַל הַנֶּפֶשׁ מִתּוֹרָה מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם שֶׁהִיא תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב, וְכֵן לַגּוּף מַאֲכָלוֹ לֶחֶם מִן הַשָּׁמָיִם; וְהַכְּנִיסָה לָאָרֶץ הוּא שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מַאֲכָל לַגּוּף לֶחֶם מִן הָאָרֶץ וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת בְּנֵי אָדָם, וְכָךְ מַאֲכַל הַנֶּפֶשׁ וְחַיּוּתָהּ — תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה וְחָכְמַת בְּנֵי אָדָם, וְהוּא פְּרִי הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב.
records.targetEnglish: In the life of the soul, it is precisely analogous to the Oral Torah: teachings that people generate of themselves through their intellect, while knowing that they come from God. They are then called “Oral Torah”; but when one does not know that they come from God, they are called “external wisdom,” corresponding to the land of the nations. For bodily life and the life of the soul are one matter, since they are clothed in one another; each simply has a different garment and appearance. Bodily life comes from food, drink, and the affairs of this world, from which the body was created; the soul’s life comes from wisdom and Torah, from which it was created, as explained. As our Sages said in Shir HaShirim Rabbah: every reference to eating and drinking in that scroll speaks of words of Torah, which are the soul’s food. So it was with Israel in the wilderness: the soul’s food came from Torah from heaven, which is the Written Torah, and the body’s food likewise was bread from heaven. Entry into the land means that the body’s food will be bread from the earth, through human effort; similarly, the soul’s food and life will be the Oral Torah and human wisdom, which is the fruit of the Written Torah.
records.explanation: The analogy explains why the land and Oral Torah appear together in this paragraph. Both require a person to act through ordinary human capacities while recognizing their divine source. The preceding lines in Likkutei Maamarim explicitly describe plowing, sowing, and harvesting; the selected passage then maps that bodily labor onto intellectual labor. Its account of Oral Torah includes both human thinking and dependence on the Written Torah. It does not treat an independently imagined idea as Torah merely because it feels inspired.

records.themeTitle: The labor that receives wisdom begins in a persistent desire for it
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok calls the result of Torah labor a “finding” because the insight exceeds what the person could have planned or produced. Machshavot Charutz explains how a seeker can already be called wise before receiving that wisdom.
records.originHebrew: שֶׁכְּשֶׁיָּגַע בְּחָכְמַת לִבּוֹ וְכָל כֹּחַ הַשָּׂגָתוֹ לְהַשִּׂיג, עַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: "יָגַעְתָּ וּמָצָאתָ – תַּאֲמִין" (מְגִילָּה ו:). וְיָדוּעַ בְּפֵירוּשׁ לְשׁוֹן "מָצָאתָ", דִּמְצִיאָה הוּא בְּהֶסַּח הַדַּעַת (סַנְהֶדְרִין צז.), שֶׁהַשָּׂגָתוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ דֶּרֶךְ מְצִיאָה, שֶׁמַּשִּׂיג מַה שֶּׁלֹּא יָגַע עָלֶיהָ כְּלָל; כִּי קוֹדֶם הַהַשָּׂגָה לֹא יָכוֹל לְיַגֵּעַ עַצְמוֹ עַל הַשָּׂגָה כָּזוֹ כְּלָל, רַק לְמִי שֶׁיָּגַע בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה, הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁפִּיעַ וְנוֹתֵן בּוֹ חָכְמָה לְהַשִּׂיג גַּם מַה שֶּׁלְּמַעְלָה מֵחָכְמָתוֹ וְהַשָּׂגָתוֹ,
records.originEnglish: When one labors with the wisdom of his heart and the full power of his understanding to attain it, of this they said, “You have labored and found—believe it.” The meaning of “found” is known: a finding occurs outside one’s directed attention. His later attainment comes as a finding, for he attains something for which he did not labor at all; before attaining it, he could not have directed his labor toward such an attainment. Rather, to one who labors in words of Torah, God grants and imparts wisdom to attain even what is above his own wisdom and understanding.
records.targetHebrew: וְהָעִיקָּר הוּא הַחֵשֶׁק וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בִּמְגִלָּה ו׳ עַמּוּד ב׳: ״׳יָגַעְתִּי וְלֹא מָצָאתִי׳ — אַל תַּאֲמִין״ כִּי כָּל הַשָּׂגָה וּמַדְרֵגָה אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי הַיְגִיעָה, שֶׁהוּא עַל יְדֵי הַחֵשֶׁק וְהַהִשְׁתּוֹקְקוּת שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָאָדָם לְדָבָר זֶה, וְלֹא יָנוּחַ וְלֹא יִשְׁקוֹט עַד שֶׁיִּמְצָא וְגוּף הַהַשָּׂגָה נִקְרָא ״מְצִיאָה״, דִּבְאֶמֶת ״ה׳ יִתֵּן חָכְמָה״ (מִשְׁלֵי ב:ו) וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְאָדָם לְהַשִּׂיג שׁוּם דָּבָר בְּכֹחוֹ וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ כְּלָל אֶלָּא דְּהוּא ״יָהֵב חָכְמְתָא לְחַכִּימִין״ (דָּנִיֵּאל ב:כא), וְאֵיךְ אֶפְשָׁר לִהְיוֹת חַכִּימִין מִקּוֹדֶם אֲבָל זֶהוּ כָּל חָכְמַת הָאָדָם: מַה שֶּׁחוֹשֵׁק לִשְׁקוֹד וּלְיַיגֵּעַ לְהַשִּׂיג הַחָכְמָה וְהַחָכְמָה קוֹרְאָה בְּרֹאשׁ הוֹמִיּוֹת: ״אֲנִי אֹהֲבַי אֵהָב וּמְשַׁחֲרַי יִמְצָאֻנְנִי״ (מִשְׁלֵי ח:יז)
records.targetEnglish: The essential thing is the longing, as it says in Megillah: “I have labored and have not found—do not believe it.” Every attainment and spiritual level comes only through labor, which comes from a person’s longing and yearning for that matter: he will neither rest nor be quiet until he finds it. The attainment itself is called a “finding,” for in truth “the Lord gives wisdom,” and a person cannot attain anything through his own power and effort at all. Yet “He gives wisdom to the wise”—how can they already be wise beforehand? This is the whole of human wisdom: the desire to apply oneself and labor to attain wisdom. Wisdom calls at the head of the crowded places: “I love those who love me, and those who seek me diligently will find me.”
records.explanation: The source identifies what belongs to the seeker before the gift arrives: a desire that becomes sustained effort. This resolves the apparent circularity of God giving wisdom to someone already wise. In the present paragraph, the same structure explains why the result can be both consequent upon labor and beyond the laborer’s prior grasp. The “finding” does not dispense with study; it describes the disproportion between the person’s faithful seeking and the wisdom ultimately granted.

records.themeTitle: The depth of Torah and the visibility of revelation are different measures
records.themeSummary: The second Temple can lack the first Temple’s manifest prophetic revelation while becoming the setting for a greater disclosure of Torah’s hidden teachings. Tzidkat HaTzadik states the distinction between depth of wisdom and clarity of revelation directly.
records.originHebrew: וְרָז וְסוֹד שֶׁל תּוֹרָה זֶה, הוּא הַמִּסְטוֹרִין וְסוֹדוֹת דְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁהִתְחִיל וְנִתְחַדֵּשׁ בְּאוֹתוֹ דּוֹר, עַל יְדֵי חֶשְׁקָם וִיגִיעָתָם הָעֲצוּמָה לְהִשְׁתַּדֵּל בָּהּ. וּשְׁכִינָה בְּקֹדֶשׁ הַקֳּדָשִׁים, שֶׁנִּקְרָא "חֲדַר הַמִּטּוֹת", מִשְׁכַּן הַכְּרוּבִים "כִּמְעַר אִישׁ וְלֹיוֹת" (מְלָכִים א ז׳:ל״ו), שֶׁהוּא יִחוּד הַגָּמוּר דְּקוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא וּשְׁכִינְתֵּיהּ, שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹכֵן בְּתוֹךְ הַלְּבָבוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מַמָּשׁ, דְּזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ "יְכַוֵּין אֶת לִבּוֹ כְּנֶגֶד בֵּית קֹדֶשׁ הַקֳּדָשִׁים" (בְּרָכוֹת ל.) כַּיָּדוּעַ, מִשָּׁם הָיָה הַשָּׂגַת הַנְּבִיאִים.
records.originEnglish: This mystery and secret of Torah consists of the hidden teachings and secrets of the Oral Torah, which began and were newly disclosed in that generation through their longing and immense labor to pursue it. The Shekhinah in the Holy of Holies, called the “bedchamber,” the dwelling of the cherubim “like a man joined with his companion,” is the complete union of the Holy One and His Shekhinah, in which God dwells within the hearts of Israel themselves. This is the meaning of “he should direct his heart toward the Holy of Holies,” as is known; from there came the prophets’ attainment.
records.targetHebrew: וְאָז לְצוֹרֶךְ בִּנְיַן בַּיִת שֵׁנִי שֶׁהָיָה הִסְתַּלְּקוּת הַנְּבוּאָה, וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם מְפוֹרָשׁ בְּפִרְקֵי הֵיכָלוֹת (פֶּרֶק כז וּפֶרֶק כט) כִּי עִיקַּר רָזֵי תּוֹרָה לֹא נִגְלָה אֶלָּא בְּבַיִת שֵׁנִי, וְכַנּוֹדָע דְּאָז יְסוֹד תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה מֵאַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה. וּבֶאֱמֶת "חָכָם עָדִיף מִנָּבִיא", עַיֵּין בָּרַמְבַּ״ן פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (יב.) הַטַּעַם, דְּנוֹבֵעַ מִמָּקוֹם יוֹתֵר גָּדוֹל, וּבַזֹּהַר שְׁמוֹת (ו סוֹף עַמּוּד ב) כִּי הוּא תְּמִידִי. רַק דְּהַנְּבוּאָה הוּא הִתְגַּלּוּת מַאֲמַר ה' בְּבֵירוּר, וְהַשָּׂגָה דְּחָכְמָה הוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם.
records.targetEnglish: At that time, in preparation for the building of the second Temple, prophecy was departing. Nevertheless, the Chapters of the Heavenly Palaces explicitly state that the principal mysteries of Torah were revealed only in the second Temple period; and it is known that the foundation of the Oral Torah then came from the Men of the Great Assembly. In truth, “a sage is greater than a prophet.” See Ramban in the first chapter of Bava Batra: the reason is that it flows from a higher place; and in the Zohar, Shemot, the reason is that it is continual. Yet prophecy is the clear revelation of the Lord’s utterance, while the attainment of wisdom occurs in concealment.
records.explanation: The final qualification prevents “greater” from becoming a claim that the sage sees more openly than the prophet. Rav Tzadok distinguishes the source and depth of attained wisdom from the clarity with which divine speech is perceived. This is exactly what allows the present discussion to describe the loss of one form of revelation alongside the growth of Oral Torah through love and labor. The comparison concerns these modes of attainment, rather than a general ranking of every sage above every prophet.

records.themeTitle: Moses’ gift lets each learner uncover a personal portion through difficulty
records.themeSummary: The gift of pilpul—understanding one matter from another—connects Moses’ Torah with the understanding in each person’s heart. Sod Yesharim explains how questions and contradictions uncover that inherited share.
records.originHebrew: וְאַחַר כָּךְ שָׁם נֶאֱמַר: "כְּתָב לְךָ אֶת הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה" (שָׁם כז), וְדָרְשׁוּ מִזֶּה (נְדָרִים לח.): דְּלֹא נִיתְּנוּ אֶלָּא לְמֹשֶׁה וּלְזַרְעוֹ, וְהוּא נָהַג טוֹבַת עַיִן וּנְתָנָהּ לְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל; וּמַסִּיק: דְּהַיְינוּ לְפִלְפּוּלָא, וּפֵירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י: לְהָבִין דָּבָר מִתּוֹךְ דָּבָר, וְהַיְינוּ תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה.
records.originEnglish: Afterward it says there, “Write for yourself these words.” From this they expounded that they were given only to Moses and his descendants, but he acted generously and gave them to all Israel. The conclusion is that this refers to pilpul, which Rashi explains as understanding one matter from another; this is the Oral Torah.
records.targetHebrew: וזה הרווחא שמעתתא היוצא אחר כמה קושיות וסתירות ונקרא פלפולא דאורייתא שמשה רבינו נהג בה טובת עין ונתנה לישראל היינו שמאוד בהצנע קבע מ"ר בעומק הלב של כל פרט נפש מישראל כל הד"ת וכל פרט נפש יכול שפיר למצוא אחר פלפול יגיעתו החלק שיש לו בהדברי תורה בשורשו וכדאיתא במדרש (צו פ' ט) המובא לעיל (אות מ') שאמר העם הארץ לר' ינאי ירותתי גבך וכו' תורה צוה לנו משה מורשה קהלת ינאי אין כתיב כאן אלא מורשה קהלת יעקב להורות שהד"ת שנתן מ"ר לישראל יש בה חלק לכל פרט נפש אפי' הקטן ביותר
records.targetEnglish: This expanded understanding of a teaching, which emerges after many questions and contradictions, is called the Torah’s pilpul, in which Moses our teacher acted generously and gave it to Israel. This means that, very secretly, Moses established all the words of Torah in the depths of the heart of every individual soul in Israel. After the searching labor of his pilpul, each individual soul can indeed find the portion of the words of Torah that belongs to him at his root. As stated in the Midrash cited above, the unlearned person said to Rabbi Yannai, “My inheritance is with you.” “Moses commanded us the Torah, an inheritance of the congregation of Yannai” is not written here, but “an inheritance of the congregation of Jacob.” This teaches that the words of Torah Moses gave to Israel contain a share for every individual soul, even the least of them.
records.explanation: Both texts start from the same teaching in Nedarim about Moses’ generosity. Sod Yesharim explains its effect: the gift implants an inheritance in every Jewish soul, and disciplined questioning brings the learner’s portion into expression. That helps explain why Rav Tzadok immediately turns to what is written on the heart and to the understanding particular to each sage. The parallel supports this movement from Moses to the individual learner; it does not identify the transmitter of Rav Tzadok’s later teaching, “write yourself,” which remains unattributed in his text.

records.themeTitle: An initial illumination shows a possibility that still has to be acquired
records.themeSummary: A first encounter with light may be vivid without yet becoming a stable acquisition of the heart. Resisei Layla explains both the fading of the initial fervor and the purpose that the first glimpse continues to serve.
records.originHebrew: וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּעִיקַּר הַהִתְגַּלּוּת הָיָה בִּקְרִיעַת יַם סוּף, שֶׁאָמְרוּ: דְּרָאֲתָה שִׁפְחָה מַה שֶּׁלֹּא רָאָה יְחֶזְקֵאל (מְכִילְתָּא בְּשַׁלַּח); רַק שֶׁהָיָה בִּרְאִיָּה לְבַד וְלֹא בְּקִנְיָן קָבוּעַ בַּלֵּב. וְהַסָּלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ דִּ"בִּרְאִיָּה בְּעָלְמָא קָנֵי" כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרֵישׁ בָּבָא מְצִיעָא (ב:), הַיְינוּ שֶׁבְּדַעַת בְּנֵי אָדָם, כְּשֶׁמַּשִּׂיג הַדָּבָר בִּרְאִיָּה, חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁכְּבָר הִשִּׂיגוֹ וְשֶׁהוּא בְּקִנְיָן; וְהָאֱמֶת אֵינוֹ כֵן, דְּאַחַר כָּךְ בָּאוּ לִרְפִידִים – לְרִפְיוֹן יָדָם מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו.), וּמִיָּד בָּא עֲמָלֵק הַמְקַטְרֵג.
records.originEnglish: I heard that the principal revelation was at the splitting of the Sea, of which they said that a maidservant saw what Ezekiel did not see. Yet it was only a vision, not an acquired possession fixed in the heart. The initial supposition that “one acquires through seeing alone,” as stated at the beginning of Bava Metzia, means that people think that when they apprehend something by seeing it, they have already attained it and possess it. In truth this is not so: afterward they came to Rephidim, to a slackening of their hands in Torah, and immediately Amalek the accuser came.
records.targetHebrew: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי, דְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה הוּא בְּקִנְיָן מַה שֶׁהָיָה בִּקְרִיעַת יַם סוּף בִּרְאִיָּה, דְּהָרְאִיָּה אֵינוֹ קִנְיָן בַּלֵּב. רַק לְפִי הַסָּלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ בַּגְּמָרָא רֵישׁ בָּבָא מְצִיעָא: ״בִּרְאִיָּה בְּעָלְמָא קָנֵי״, הַיְינוּ דְּסָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ דְּמַחֲשֶׁבֶת בְּנֵי אָדָם הוּא כֵּן. וּקְרִיעַת יַם סוּף הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתַב בָּרוֹקֵחַ: ״אֵין חֹזֶק כַּחֲסִידוּת בִּתְחִלָּתוֹ״. וְאַחַר כָּךְ נִשְׁקָע אוֹתוֹ חֵשֶׁק, כִּי הוּא רְאִיָּה לְבַד, וְצָרִיךְ לַחֲזוֹר וּלְעוֹרְרוֹ עַד שֶׁיָּבוֹא לִהְיוֹת קִנְיָן בַּלֵּב. וּלְעוֹלָם הָרְאִיָּה הוּא כְּפִי מַה שֶׁהוּא מוּכָן לְהַשִּׂיג בְּקִנְיָן, מַרְאִין לוֹ תְּחִלָּה: ״לָזֶה אַתָּה מוּכָן״.
records.targetEnglish: As I heard: the giving of the Torah made an acquired possession of what had been a vision at the splitting of the Sea, for seeing is not an acquisition in the heart. Only according to the initial supposition in the Gemara at the beginning of Bava Metzia does “one acquire through seeing alone”; that is, this is what people initially think. The splitting of the Sea accords with the Rokeach’s statement, “There is no strength like the devotion of the beginning.” Afterward that longing subsides, because it was only a vision, and one must return and awaken it until it becomes an acquired possession in the heart. The vision always corresponds to what the person is prepared to attain as a possession: he is shown at the beginning, “For this you are prepared.”
records.explanation: The added point is the function of the first glimpse: it shows a real capacity that has not yet been made stable. Its fading therefore calls for renewed labor and awakening. This helps distinguish Rav Tzadok’s “vision” from an illusion, while also explaining why vividness alone is insufficient. The present section later applies the distinction repeatedly: once one level is acquired, a higher light may again be known first through faith and concealment. The quoted source supplies the structure of the first transition, from glimpsed possibility to acquired life.
